feed.title: The Larger World Archive
feed.subtitle: Hidden-world claims, their sources, and what the evidence says.

entry.title: AI Existential Risk
entry.summary: Serious researchers disagree about whether advanced AI poses a civilisational risk. What the argument actually claims, what would count as evidence, and why the debate is stuck.

entry.title: Algorithmic Fairness
entry.summary: Demographic parity, equalised odds and calibration are each defensible, and proven to be jointly impossible when base rates differ. The real question is which error you are willing to distribute unevenly.

entry.title: Aliens, Area 51 & the UFO Files
entry.summary: Project Blue Book's 12,618 sightings, the Roswell balloon record, the 2004 Nimitz encounter, the 2021 government UAP assessment — and what 'unidentified' actually means.

entry.title: Alzheimer's
entry.summary: The amyloid cascade, the two drugs that finally worked a little, the retracted paper, and the competing infection, vascular and metabolic accounts — weighed rather than asserted.

entry.title: AMOC Tipping
entry.summary: The Atlantic overturning circulation is weakening and will weaken further. Whether it can collapse this century is a live, high-stakes and genuinely uncertain question.

entry.title: Did Anastasia Survive?
entry.summary: The Anastasia survival story: the 1918 execution, Anna Anderson, the 1991 exhumations, and the mitochondrial DNA that ended it.

entry.title: Ancient Astronauts
entry.summary: The ancient astronaut hypothesis: its lineage from Charles Fort to Chariots of the Gods, Sitchin's Nibiru, and what each famous exhibit — Palenque, Nazca, Puma Punku, the Dogon, crystal skulls — actually is.

entry.title: The Aquatic Ape
entry.summary: A human ancestor that took to the water would explain hairlessness, upright posture and the diving reflex in one stroke. The fossil record, the comparative anatomy and the genetics each say otherwise, and the charitable version of the idea is a different claim.

entry.title: The Arrow of Time
entry.summary: The microscopic laws run equally well backwards; the world does not. The leading explanation is a low-entropy initial condition, which nobody can yet explain.

entry.title: The Backrooms
entry.summary: The Backrooms: the 2019 4chan post, where the yellow-wallpaper photo came from, the “levels” lore, and why liminal-space horror works.

entry.title: The Bicameral Mind
entry.summary: Julian Jaynes's 1976 theory that ancient people had no introspective consciousness and heard their own thoughts as gods' voices — what it claims, and why it has no neurological support.

entry.title: Bitcoin as Digital Gold
entry.summary: The case for bitcoin as a scarce, bearer, censorship-resistant store of value, the case against it as volatile, energy-intensive and functionally a lottery ticket, and the data in between.

entry.title: The Black Knight
entry.summary: The Black Knight satellite: the 1998 shuttle photograph, what the object actually was, where the 13,000-year claim came from, and the real radio mystery it gets mixed up with.

entry.title: Black Swans
entry.summary: Taleb's black swan is rare, consequential and explainable only afterwards. The concept names a real failure of forecasting; it is also frequently used to avoid the discipline of forecasting at all.

entry.title: Boltzmann Brains
entry.summary: Boltzmann brains: why an eternally fluctuating universe predicts more lone minds than whole civilisations, how cosmologists use this as a reductio, and what it does not prove.

entry.title: The Bosnian Pyramids
entry.summary: The Bosnian pyramids claim: Visočica hill, Semir Osmanagić, the geology of sedimentary bedding, and the archaeologists' formal condemnation.

entry.title: Broken Windows Policing
entry.summary: Disorder enforcement was sold as the reason crime fell in the 1990s. The natural experiments suggest the causal story is much weaker, and the costs were borne unevenly.

entry.title: The Chinese Room
entry.summary: Searle's thought experiment is the most cited argument in the philosophy of AI. Four decades of replies have not settled whether it shows anything about machines, or only about the intuition.

entry.title: Cold Fusion
entry.summary: Two electrochemists announced tabletop fusion on 23 March 1989. Within six months the effect had failed to replicate, and thirty-seven years later there is still a conference, a journal and no accepted mechanism.

entry.title: The Contact Hypothesis
entry.summary: Allport's four conditions for contact that reduces prejudice have strong meta-analytic support. The argument is about whether real-world contact meets them, and what happens when it does not.

entry.title: Creationism and the Alternatives to Darwin
entry.summary: Creationism, intelligent design and other alternatives to Darwinian evolution, scored claim by claim: what the fossils, the dating and the lab experiments actually show, and where the real scientific arguments are.

entry.title: Cryptids
entry.summary: The cryptid file: Bigfoot and bear populations, the confessed Loch Ness hoax and its eDNA survey, the Yeti footprint, Mokele-mbembe, and the pattern behind the sightings.

entry.title: Curses
entry.summary: The mummy's curse tested as a cohort study, the Amityville haunting and its collapse in court, and the Hope Diamond's curse as a 20th-century newspaper invention.

entry.title: The Dark Forest
entry.summary: Liu Cixin's dark forest answer to the Fermi paradox: the two axioms, the chain of suspicion, and why a brilliant fictional premise is not a scientific finding.

entry.title: Dark Matter
entry.summary: Why astronomers are confident most mass is invisible, and where WIMPs, axions, sterile neutrinos and primordial black holes each stand after decades of null results.

entry.title: The Dead Internet Theory
entry.summary: The Dead Internet Theory: where it came from on Agora Road, what the bot and AI-content data really shows, and which parts of the claim survive contact with evidence.

entry.title: Deep Web & Dark Web
entry.summary: Surface web, deep web, dark web: the definitions from the Congressional Research Service, how Tor works, real takedowns, and a directory of legitimate hidden-away archives.

entry.title: Democratic Peace
entry.summary: The dyadic finding is one of the most replicated in international relations. Whether it is caused by norms, institutions, shared interests or Cold War alliances is still argued, and the edge cases are instructive.

entry.title: The Dinosaur Extinction
entry.summary: An asteroid hit the Yucatán 66 million years ago and three quarters of species died. The argument about whether the impact or the Deccan volcanoes did it is now mostly an argument about timing, and the timing has been measured.

entry.title: Unresolved Disappearances
entry.summary: Seven unresolved disappearances — MH370, the Mary Celeste, Amelia Earhart, the Sodder children, the Joyita, Percy Fawcett — with the evidence, the leading explanations and what is genuinely unknown.

entry.title: The Doomsday Argument
entry.summary: If your birth rank among all humans is unremarkable, the human story is probably closer to its end than its beginning. The inference is either profound or an artefact of how you count observers.

entry.title: Dragons & Dinosaurs
entry.summary: The 2013 phylogenetic study tracing dragon myths to a single origin 75,000 years ago, fossil-inspired folklore, and the creationist claim that dragons were dinosaurs.

entry.title: Dunbar's Number
entry.summary: The claim that human groups have a cognitive ceiling near 150 comes from primate brain sizes. The number is famous, the confidence interval is enormous, and online life has turned it into a test case.

entry.title: Dyatlov Pass
entry.summary: The 1959 Dyatlov Pass incident: the documented facts, the theories from infrasound to secret weapons, and the 2021 avalanche modelling that closed most of the case.

entry.title: Dyson Swarms
entry.summary: Freeman Dyson's point was not that anyone would build a shell. It was that a growing civilisation must radiate waste heat, and that this is what a telescope could see.

entry.title: Echo Chambers
entry.summary: Feed algorithms were accused of building bubbles that drive polarisation. When researchers ran randomised experiments on the platforms themselves, the picture got stranger and more interesting.

entry.title: The Ediacaran Organisms
entry.summary: Between 575 and 539 million years ago, soft-bodied organisms unlike anything alive today covered the sea floor. What they were is still argued over.

entry.title: The Egg
entry.summary: Andy Weir's 2009 short story The Egg: what it actually says, how it became “the egg theory”, and where the one-soul idea comes from in philosophy and religion.

entry.title: Ego Depletion
entry.summary: The claim that self-control draws on a limited resource, depleted by use and restored by glucose, collapsed in large preregistered replications.

entry.title: Enshittification
entry.summary: Doctorow's four-stage account of platform decay, the court records that support it, and the reasons economists have been slow to adopt the word.

entry.title: The First Eukaryote
entry.summary: Mitochondria were once free-living bacteria. What is settled about that merger, what is not, and why the host cell's identity is still argued over.

entry.title: Fast Radio Bursts
entry.summary: Millisecond flashes of radio energy from other galaxies, first dismissed as a microwave oven and now observed in their thousands. The phenomenon is documented; the source of most of them is still open.

entry.title: The Firewall Paradox
entry.summary: Entanglement, equivalence and unitarity cannot all hold at a black hole horizon. The argument, the proposed escapes, and why it matters for quantum gravity.

entry.title: Flat Earth & the Firmament
entry.summary: The flat Earth disc, ice rim, firmament dome and accelerating plane — the movement's own arguments, the Bedford Level experiment that started it, and the measurements that ended it.

entry.title: Noah, Gilgamesh & the Great Flood
entry.summary: The Gilgamesh flood tablet and its relation to Genesis, flood stories worldwide, the Black Sea deluge hypothesis and its refutation, and why flood geology fails.

entry.title: The Free Energy Principle
entry.summary: A single mathematical principle is said to explain perception, action, learning and life itself. Its defenders call it the closest thing neuroscience has to a unifying law; its critics call it unfalsifiable, and both have a point.

entry.title: FTX
entry.summary: How a crypto exchange worth $32 billion collapsed in ten days, where the customer deposits went, and what the trial established.

entry.title: Fusion on the Grid
entry.summary: A laser fusion experiment released more energy than it absorbed in 2022. That is a real milestone and a long way from electricity, which the coverage did not always say.

entry.title: Gaia
entry.summary: Lovelock and Margulis's Gaia hypothesis: what it proposed, the Daisyworld model, the natural-selection objection, and how Earth system science kept the feedbacks and dropped the goddess.

entry.title: Geographic Determinism
entry.summary: Diamond's argument that geography set the fate of continents is one of the most influential ideas in popular history. Economists have spent thirty years testing it against the alternative.

entry.title: The Giant Trees
entry.summary: The 'Silicon Forest' claim that Devils Tower and columnar basalt are petrified giant trees — and the cooling-contraction geology that explains them, plus the genuinely enormous trees that exist.

entry.title: Giants
entry.summary: Giants in the Bible and world myth, Josephus on giant bones, the 1869 Cardiff Giant hoax, and what archaeology and fossil proboscideans actually show.

entry.title: Göbekli Tepe
entry.summary: What the excavation actually found at Göbekli Tepe, why the 11,500-year date matters, and which of the famous claims the evidence does not support.

entry.title: The Great Filter
entry.summary: Hanson's argument that some step from chemistry to galactic civilisation is very improbable, and why finding simple life elsewhere would be bad news.

entry.title: The Great Stagnation
entry.summary: Productivity growth in rich countries fell sharply after 1970 and has not recovered. Whether that means ideas are exhausted or that the gains moved off the balance sheet is a live argument.

entry.title: Growth Mindset
entry.summary: Believing that ability can grow is a defensible idea with a small, real effect. Believing it is a lever that raises attainment for everyone is a claim that failed its largest test.

entry.title: The Gut–Brain Axis
entry.summary: The microbiome influences the brain through immune, neural and metabolic routes. What is established, what is correlation, and why the headlines outrun the trials.

entry.title: Did Hitler Escape?
entry.summary: The claim that Hitler fled to Argentina: the dental evidence, the repeated Soviet exhumations, the declassified FBI files, and why historians reject the escape story.

entry.title: Hollow Earth & the Inner Sun
entry.summary: Three centuries of hollow Earth theory: Halley's concentric shells, Symmes's polar holes, the Koreshan colony, the inner sun, the Byrd diary hoax, and the seismic data that rules it out.

entry.title: The Holographic Principle
entry.summary: What AdS/CFT actually says, why it is the most cited idea in quantum gravity, and why 'we live in a hologram' is a much stronger claim than the mathematics supports.

entry.title: The Hubble Tension
entry.summary: The local and early-universe expansion rates differ by more than their error bars. What the measurements are, why JWST did not resolve it, and what could.

entry.title: Hyperloop Feasibility
entry.summary: A capsule in a low-pressure tube at 1,200 km/h is not physically impossible. It is a set of unglamorous problems — expansion, alignment, evacuation, capacity — that have ended every attempt so far.

entry.title: Beyond the Ice Wall
entry.summary: The world-beyond-the-ice-wall claim: its origin in flat Earth and hollow Earth, Operation Highjump, the Antarctic Treaty, the Byrd missing diary, and what Antarctica is actually like.

entry.title: IIT versus Global Workspace
entry.summary: Integrated information theory and global neuronal workspace make different predictions about where consciousness lives in the brain. A large adversarial collaboration tested both.

entry.title: Inflation versus a Bounce
entry.summary: Inflation explains why the universe is so smooth and flat, and predicts the spectrum of the cosmic microwave background. Why some cosmologists still look for a bounce instead.

entry.title: The Jevons Paradox
entry.summary: Making something cheaper per unit tends to increase how much of it is used. The evidence, the rebound effect, and why this is an argument about magnitude, not direction.

entry.title: Kardashev Bottlenecks
entry.summary: A growing technological civilisation should fill its galaxy in a few million years. Nothing has. The candidate bottlenecks are thermodynamic, logistical, or behavioural — and each predicts something observable.

entry.title: The Larger Globe
entry.summary: Three distinct 'larger globe' theories — expanding Earth, a secretly enormous Earth, and the concave Earth — with their proponents, evidence and the measurements that tested them.

entry.title: Last Thursdayism
entry.summary: Last Thursdayism, Gosse's Omphalos, Russell's five-minute world: the argument that any evidence for an old universe can be planted, and why unfalsifiability is the point.

entry.title: Lead and Crime
entry.summary: The lead-crime hypothesis: why removing lead from petrol correlates with falling violent crime two decades later, and where the causal argument is still contested.

entry.title: Learning Styles
entry.summary: The idea that children learn better when taught in their preferred mode — visual, auditory, kinaesthetic — is one of the most widely held beliefs in education and one of the most thoroughly tested negatives in psychology.

entry.title: The Lindy Effect
entry.summary: A book that has lasted fifty years will probably last another fifty. The rule is intuitive, occasionally useful, and rests on a hazard rate that has to be decreasing — which is an empirical claim, not a law.

entry.title: Lost Continents
entry.summary: Who invented Lemuria and why, how Mu entered the occult, the Theosophical root races, and the real drowned lands — Zealandia, Sundaland, Doggerland — that geology actually confirms.

entry.title: MAD Stability
entry.summary: No great-power war since 1945 is the strongest evidence for nuclear deterrence. The declassified near-misses are the strongest evidence that the mechanism is fragile.

entry.title: Magnetic Monopoles
entry.summary: Dirac showed a single magnetic monopole would explain why electric charge is quantised. Decades of searches have found none, and theory still expects them somewhere.

entry.title: Magnetoreception
entry.summary: Animals navigate by the Earth's magnetic field. That much is settled by decades of behavioural experiments. How a biological cell measures a field a hundred thousand times weaker than a fridge magnet is not.

entry.title: The Mandela Effect
entry.summary: The Mandela Effect: who named it, the standard examples, and the psychology — false memory, confabulation, source confusion and schema theory — versus the parallel-universe claim.

entry.title: Many Worlds
entry.summary: Hugh Everett's relative-state formulation: what many-worlds really says, why it is mainstream rather than fringe, and why it is not the “every decision splits reality” story.

entry.title: Market Efficiency
entry.summary: The efficient market hypothesis is not one claim but three, and the evidence is different for each. Its defenders say the anomalies are the interesting part.

entry.title: Mass Hysteria
entry.summary: The 1518 dancing plague in Strasbourg, the 1962 Tanganyika laughter epidemic, Salem 1692 and the psychology of mass psychogenic illness — with the documentary record.

entry.title: The Median Voter Theorem
entry.summary: With one issue dimension and single-peaked preferences, two competing parties both move to the median. Real elections have many dimensions, primaries, and voters who stay home — which is where the theorem stops predicting.

entry.title: Minimum Wage Effects
entry.summary: Does a higher wage floor cost jobs? Two decades of local natural experiments have moved the consensus, and the argument has moved with it — to the size of the effect and who bears it.

entry.title: Modern Monetary Theory
entry.summary: MMT's central claim is that a government which issues its own currency cannot go bankrupt, only inflate. The argument is about where the real limit sits, and how fast you find out.

entry.title: MOND
entry.summary: Milgrom's modified dynamics explains galaxy rotation without dark matter, and struggles with clusters. How the theory works, where it wins, and where it does not.

entry.title: How the Moon Formed
entry.summary: The giant-impact hypothesis explains the Moon's small iron core and Earth's spin. Isotopic measurements have made the standard version harder to defend.

entry.title: The End of Moore’s Law
entry.summary: Transistor counts kept doubling for fifty years. That specific trend is over. What replaced it — packaging, specialised chips, new architectures — is the real story.

entry.title: The Muon's Wobble
entry.summary: The muon's magnetic moment disagrees with one calculation of the Standard Model and agrees with another. Which one is right decides whether new physics is needed.

entry.title: Mutants & “Superpowers”
entry.summary: Real 'superpower' variants: LRP5 unbreakable bones, EPAS1 altitude adaptation, malaria resistance, tetrachromacy — plus gigantism, radiation myths and why 'mutant' is a misleading word.

entry.title: Unknown Mysteries
entry.summary: How two famous mysteries were made: Vincent Gaddis and Charles Berlitz on the Bermuda Triangle, Lawrence Kusche's 1975 demolition, and what the Nazca geoglyphs were for.

entry.title: Oak Island
entry.summary: The Oak Island money pit: the 1795 discovery, the booby-trap legend, the treasure candidates, and why two centuries of excavation is itself the best evidence there is nothing there.

entry.title: Objective Collapse
entry.summary: GRW and related models make wavefunction collapse a real, physical, random event. They solve the measurement problem and make a testable prediction that experiments are closing in on.

entry.title: The Omega Point
entry.summary: Teilhard's theological endpoint and Tipler's physical version both claim history converges on a final state of infinite information. One is poetry, the other required a closed universe that the data have since ruled out.

entry.title: Open versus Closed Models
entry.summary: Open weights let anyone audit, replicate and localise a model. They also let anyone remove its safety training. Both facts are established, and they point in opposite directions.

entry.title: The Origin of Life
entry.summary: RNA world, metabolism-first, alkaline vents and warm ponds: the competing accounts of how chemistry became biology, and the experiments that separate them.

entry.title: ‘Oumuamua
entry.summary: The first object known to arrive from another star system accelerated more than gravity explains. Hydrogen iceberg, nitrogen shard, or a rock with an odd shape — and why the lightsail claim fails.

entry.title: The Panama Papers
entry.summary: The largest leak in journalism history exposed offshore structures used by politicians and billionaires. Most were legal; the point was that they were secret.

entry.title: Panpsychism
entry.summary: The view that experience is a basic feature of matter, not something that emerges from complexity. It is taken seriously by a minority of philosophers, has no test, and is not the same as saying rocks are conscious.

entry.title: Paul Is Dead
entry.summary: The 1969 “Paul is dead” rumour: the car crash that never happened, the Abbey Road barefoot clue, the backmasked voices, and why a hoax this good outlived its truth.

entry.title: Pegasus
entry.summary: NSO Group's zero-click exploit turned phones into pocket microphones. What the Pegasus Project established, and the limits of what it proved.

entry.title: Peto's Paradox
entry.summary: If cancer is a numbers game, elephants and whales should be riddled with it. They are not. The competing explanations, and what the data actually show.

entry.title: Phantom Time
entry.summary: Heribert Illig's claim that 614–911 AD was fabricated, and the five independent records — tree rings, eclipses, Chinese annals, coins, charters — that rule it out.

entry.title: Phosphine on Venus
entry.summary: A spectral line at 266.94 GHz was reported as phosphine, a gas with no obvious abiotic source on Venus. What reanalysis found, and why the claim has not died.

entry.title: Pilot-Wave Theory
entry.summary: De Broglie–Bohm theory gives every particle a definite position guided by a wavefunction. It reproduces quantum predictions exactly, and it needs a preferred frame.

entry.title: The Pixar Theory
entry.summary: Jon Negroni's 2013 Pixar Theory: the claim that every Pixar film is one continuous timeline, the evidence used, and why it is criticism rather than conspiracy.

entry.title: The Placebo Effect
entry.summary: The placebo effect is real, modest, and much narrower than either its critics or its enthusiasts claim. It works best on symptoms you have to report and worst on outcomes a machine measures.

entry.title: Planet Nine
entry.summary: Six distant objects cluster in a way that suggests a planet, or a disk, or a selection effect. The evidence for Planet Nine, the alternatives, and why it is still not found.

entry.title: Polyvagal Theory
entry.summary: A three-state model of the autonomic nervous system is taught in trauma training worldwide and rests on comparative anatomy that specialists say is wrong. It is the clearest case in this archive of a clinical framework outrunning its evidence.

entry.title: Primordial Black Holes
entry.summary: Hawking's idea that the early universe could have forged black holes of every size, and how microlensing, the CMB and LIGO have squeezed the idea without killing it.

entry.title: Prophecies
entry.summary: How end-of-the-world predictions work: the 2012 Mayan non-event, the Millerites' Great Disappointment, Festinger's cognitive dissonance study and its problems, and Nostradamus.

entry.title: Proven Conspiracies
entry.summary: MKUltra, COINTELPRO, Tuskegee, the Gulf of Tonkin, Iran-Contra and the tobacco cover-up: what was claimed, what was done, and the document that proved it.

entry.title: Punctuated Equilibrium
entry.summary: Eldredge and Gould's claim that species change in rapid bursts separated by long stasis, what the fossil record shows, and why the argument is smaller than it looks.

entry.title: Quantum Advantage
entry.summary: Quantum computers have beaten classical machines on contrived tasks, then been caught by better classical algorithms. What advantage means, and where it might hold.

entry.title: Quantum Darwinism
entry.summary: Zurek's proposal that classical reality is the set of states the environment records redundantly. Elegant, widely cited, and not yet a complete derivation.

entry.title: Quantum Oddities
entry.summary: Quantum immortality from many-worlds, and Wheeler's one-electron universe: two beautiful consequences of quantum mechanics that are argued about by physicists and misused online.

entry.title: Rational Choice Voting
entry.summary: The probability that one ballot decides an election is smaller than the chance of dying on the way to the polling station. Turnout is high anyway. The explanations are duty, expression, altruism, or a model that is simply wrong.

entry.title: Readiness Potentials and Free Will
entry.summary: Libet's experiments showed brain activity preceding the felt decision to move. What that means for free will is far less clear than the headlines say.

entry.title: The Resource Curse
entry.summary: Countries with abundant minerals and fuel grow more slowly, fight more civil wars and are less democratic on average. The mechanism, the exceptions, and why the correlation is weaker than it looks.

entry.title: The Riemann Hypothesis
entry.summary: What the Riemann Hypothesis actually claims, why the zeros of the zeta function govern the primes, how far it has been verified, and why no mathematician doubts it.

entry.title: The Lost Colony
entry.summary: Roanoke: the 1587 colony, the CROATOAN carving, the hidden fort on the 1590 map, and why the leading explanation is assimilation rather than disappearance.

entry.title: Roko's Basilisk
entry.summary: Roko's Basilisk: the 2010 LessWrong post, the decision-theory it rests on, why it is a Pascal's mugging, and why the “you are now cursed” framing is the point.

entry.title: Scaling Laws
entry.summary: Loss falls as a smooth power law in model size, data and compute. That regularity is real, useful, and often over-read as a theory of capability.

entry.title: Scarcity or Ingenuity
entry.summary: Malthus, the Club of Rome and the degrowth movement on one side; Julian Simon and two centuries of falling real commodity prices on the other. What the data can and cannot settle.

entry.title: Screen Time and Teen Mental Health
entry.summary: Is smartphone use driving a rise in adolescent distress? The correlations are tiny, the trend data are contested, and both camps overstate what the evidence can carry.

entry.title: Secret Societies
entry.summary: The real Bavarian Illuminati of Adam Weishaupt, founded 1776 and banned in 1785, Freemasonry's documented history, and how a dead secret society became a permanent conspiracy.

entry.title: Secret Tests
entry.summary: Five declassified programmes: the 1950 Navy aerosol test over San Francisco, Project Sunshine's infant tissue collection, the CIA's cat, the heart-attack gun and the 'gay bomb'.

entry.title: Secular Stagnation
entry.summary: A 1938 idea revived in 2013: rich economies may have a chronic surplus of desired saving, pushing the natural interest rate below zero and leaving demand permanently short. The evidence is good and the theory is still being rewritten.

entry.title: Who Wrote Shakespeare?
entry.summary: The Shakespeare authorship question: the candidates, the evidence from title pages, wills and contemporaries, and why stylometry and collaboration studies point to Shakespeare.

entry.title: The Silurian Hypothesis
entry.summary: Frank and Schmidt's 2018 thought experiment: what a pre-human industrial civilisation would leave in the rock record, and why the answer matters more for our own future than for the past.

entry.title: The Simpsons Predictions
entry.summary: Every famous Simpsons prediction checked against the episode and the event: 20 claims, 5 exact hits, 3 partial, 5 coincidences, 5 fakes, 2 still open — plus the films that supposedly predicted the future.

entry.title: The Simulation Hypothesis
entry.summary: Nick Bostrom's 2003 simulation argument: the three propositions, what the paper actually claims, and why “glitches in the matrix” are not evidence.

entry.title: Snowball Earth
entry.summary: Twice in the Neoproterozoic, ice reached sea level in the tropics. The evidence is in the rocks and is not seriously disputed; how the planet got out again is still argued about.

entry.title: Sonoluminescence
entry.summary: A bubble trapped in a sound field collapses and flashes light. What is known about the temperatures inside, and why the mechanism is still argued over.

entry.title: The Electromagnetic Soul
entry.summary: The electromagnetic soul theory: what EEG and MEG actually measure, how strong the brain's fields really are, and why “consciousness is an EM pattern” is a metaphor rather than a finding.

entry.title: The Space Elevator
entry.summary: The physics is elementary and the engineering is brutal: a cable from the equator to geostationary orbit needs a specific strength about fifty times better than steel, and nobody can make the fibre.

entry.title: Stochastic Parrots or World Models
entry.summary: Do large language models understand anything, or only reproduce statistical patterns? The strongest evidence on both sides, and why the question is badly posed.

entry.title: The Stoned Ape
entry.summary: Terence McKenna's stoned ape hypothesis: what he claimed about psilocybin mushrooms and human brain expansion, and what the archaeological and palaeontological record actually shows.

entry.title: Strings versus Loops
entry.summary: String theory and loop quantum gravity both claim to quantise gravity. Forty years on, neither has a confirmed experimental prediction.

entry.title: Substrate Independence
entry.summary: If mental states are functional states, their material is irrelevant and silicon will do. If consciousness depends on specific biology, it will not. No experiment currently distinguishes the two.

entry.title: Dual Suns, Dual Stars
entry.summary: The Nemesis hypothesis, the Sun's possible lost twin, why most Sun-like stars are binary, and the atmospheric optics behind photographs of 'two suns'.

entry.title: Room-Temperature Superconductivity
entry.summary: Why zero-resistance materials matter, what LK-99 and the Dias retractions actually established, and why the field keeps looking.

entry.title: Superrationality
entry.summary: Hofstadter's rule for one-shot prisoner's dilemmas: if your opponent runs the same algorithm, the only question is which algorithm to be. Elegant, and dependent on an assumption the world rarely grants.

entry.title: Supersymmetry
entry.summary: Supersymmetry would double the particle menu, unify couplings and supply dark matter. The LHC has found no superpartners, and the naturalness argument has taken the damage.

entry.title: Tabby’s Star
entry.summary: KIC 8462852 dims irregularly, by up to 22 per cent, in ways ordinary stellar variability does not explain. Dust is now the leading answer; the alien megastructure is not.

entry.title: Tartaria & the Mud Flood
entry.summary: The Tartarian Empire and mud flood theory: its Russian nationalist origins, its claims about world's fair buildings, star forts and orphan trains, and the documented record that answers each.

entry.title: Technological Unemployment
entry.summary: Automation has destroyed jobs and created others for two centuries. Whether the balance is changing now is an empirical question with disputed evidence.

entry.title: Theranos
entry.summary: How a celebrated start-up raised nearly a billion dollars on a device that could not do what it claimed, and what finally ended it.

entry.title: The Thucydides Trap
entry.summary: Graham Allison counted sixteen power transitions and twelve wars. The historical claim is striking, the coding is disputed, and the policy conclusion people draw from it is stronger than the data.

entry.title: Time Crystals
entry.summary: A phase of matter whose pattern repeats in time rather than space, predicted in 2012 and built in the lab in 2017. What exists, and what the name oversells.

entry.title: Time Paradoxes
entry.summary: The grandfather paradox, Novikov's self-consistency, closed timelike curves and white holes: what general relativity actually allows, and why none of it is a time machine.

entry.title: Turbulence
entry.summary: Why the Navier–Stokes equations resist a general theory of turbulent flow, what the Millennium Prize actually asks, and how engineering copes without one.

entry.title: The Turing Test
entry.summary: Turing proposed an operational substitute for 'can machines think?'. Chatbots now pass informal versions of it, which tells us more about the test than about the machines.

entry.title: Underwater Worlds
entry.summary: What percentage of the ocean is really unmapped, the genuine sunken cities, Plato's Atlantis in his own words, and how inner-earth lore reuses the deep sea.

entry.title: Unexplained Phenomena
entry.summary: Five genuinely unexplained cases, each with the leading hypothesis and the paper behind it: Tunguska, Hessdalen, spontaneous human combustion, the Voynich manuscript, Dyatlov Pass.

entry.title: Universal Basic Income
entry.summary: Unconditional cash has been tested in Finland, Kenya, Stockton and dozens of other places. What the trials found about work, health and money, and what they could not test.

entry.title: Urban Legends & Creepypasta
entry.summary: How internet horror is made: Slender Man's 2009 forum origin and the 2014 stabbing, the Momo hoax studied as folklore, and the 1991 crop-circle confession.

entry.title: Where Viruses Came From
entry.summary: Did viruses escape from cellular genes, degenerate from cellular life, or predate cells entirely? The evidence for each, and why the question is still open.

entry.title: The Voynich Manuscript
entry.summary: The Voynich manuscript: radiocarbon dating, the script, the failed decryptions, and why 'unsolved' is a real answer rather than a failure of nerve.

entry.title: Where Earth’s Water Came From
entry.summary: Earth formed hot and dry, yet has oceans. The deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio in comets and meteorites is the main fingerprint used to trace the delivery.

entry.title: White Holes
entry.summary: Einstein's equations allow time-reversed black holes that nothing can enter. Whether any exist, and what a white hole would look like if one did.

entry.title: The Younger Dryas Impact
entry.summary: Did a fragmented comet hit North America 12,800 years ago, trigger a millennium of cooling and wipe out the Clovis culture? The evidence is contested at every step.

entry.title: The Zoo Hypothesis
entry.summary: One answer to the Fermi paradox: advanced civilisations exist, know about us, and deliberately avoid contact. It explains the silence by positing a consensus that has to hold for billions of years.
